A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world the agent's observation shows the target shifted: the target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 columns toward higher x, wrapping around. The world, its designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet, and the starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds. With the default recipe it gets only about 32 PPO updates of 4,096 steps each. That is probably too few for a task where reward depends on exact reconstruction. Placing a brick correctly is a local, layer-specific test. The landing layer is the maximum build height under the footprint. The target cells at that layer must be missing, and any gaps left below must also be empty in the target. The starting net mixes all layers in its first 1x1 layer and never lines anything up by layer. So I test two things. The first is more and smaller updates, with fewer epochs and a longer discount horizon, on the starting net. The second is a layer-relative network. It is a shared 2D network applied to each candidate landing layer, sees the column relative to that layer, scores every placement per layer, and combines the layers with logsumexp. I train it under two recipes.

### Round 2
All three trials scored exactly 0, including training success over the last 10% of training. That held for two nets and two recipes: the baseline with about 230k steps and the layer-relative net with about 120k and 225k steps. The layer-relative net builds in the landing logic, but it uses only 1x1 convolutions before a fixed top-left footprint pool. Both nets assume that a cell's features line up with the action index for that cell. If this world differs in action layout (for example, transposed axes or a different anchor), every conv-aligned head would fail completely, which fits a flat zero. The other explanation is too few samples and too much entropy for exact builds to ever happen in training. So the +1 exact-build bonus is never seen. This round is a 2x2 design. One trial adds a head that does not depend on action layout. One spends the budget on fresh samples with 1 epoch and lower entropy. One combines both.

### Round 3
All six trials scored exactly 0, both on dev and in training. That covers two networks (the baseline and the layer-relative net), three recipes (2 epochs, 4 epochs, and 1 epoch with about 400k steps), and a head that works for any action layout. Since nothing ever succeeds, there is no +1 bonus to learn from and no differences to compare yet.

I see three possible causes:
- **The agent ends too early or never sharpens.** DONE is a single action that reliably returns 0. Placement probability is spread over many equally good bricks, so under greedy argmax DONE can win even when most of the probability is on correct placements.
- **The structured net never got many samples.** The layer-relative net has not yet been tried with the 1-epoch, high-sample recipe.
- **This world differs from the description.** The anchor or footprint layout may not match, which would break the fixed footprint pool head.

Each candidate changes one thing against r2c2's recipe (1 epoch, about 400k steps), which already ran with the baseline net.

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored exactly 0 on dev and also on training (sampled) success. That held across three architecture families and recipes from 120k to 400k steps. The world probably differs from the description in a way that local convolutions cannot absorb. The flat linear head was too weak to compensate, and more samples, entropy changes and a DONE redesign did nothing. Remapping channels is already learnable through the 1x1 stems. Anchor shifts of about one cell were covered by the 3x3 heads in r3c2. Two causes remain untested: a spatial mismatch between the observation grid and the action grid (transpose or flip), and a more arbitrary cell mapping. The last round tests both. One candidate adds explicit flipped and transposed copies of the features to the head. One uses attention with learned positions, which can learn any mapping. One combines the two. Any nonzero score beats the baseline.
